Use the data only for the audit, keep it in a protected folder, and do not put PANs, accounts or names of individuals in the report. Use dealer IDs and document numbers instead. A dealer named in a list of flags has not been found guilty of anything. @sec-privacy explains how to mask and pseudonymise identifiers, and how to match lists with another department without sharing them.
:::

## What earlier chapters add {#sec-tax-earlier}

Several tests from earlier chapters apply directly. We run each in a few lines, and the chapters cited explain them in full.

**Benford's law**, @sec-benford. Turnovers of many dealers of many sizes should follow Benford's law for first digits.

```{r}
first_digit <- returns |>
  filter(turnover > 0) |>
  mutate(digit = turnover %/% 10^floor(log10(turnover))) |>
  count(digit) |>
  mutate(actual = n / sum(n), benford = log10(1 + 1 / digit))

round(mean(abs(first_digit$actual - first_digit$benford)), 4)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
mad <- round(mean(abs(first_digit$actual - first_digit$benford)), 4)
```

The mean absolute deviation is `r mad`, which Nigrini's table in @sec-benford counts as `r if (mad < 0.006) "close conformity" else if (mad < 0.012) "acceptable conformity" else if (mad < 0.015) "marginal conformity" else "nonconformity"`. Across a whole State, Benford's law rarely points to one dealer. It is more useful for one large dealer's invoices.

**Round numbers**, @sec-nigrini-round. Real sales rarely come to an exact lakh. A dealer who declares round figures month after month is likely estimating them.

```{r}
round_returns <- returns |>
  filter(turnover > 0) |>
  summarise(returns = n(), round_lakh = sum(turnover %% 1e5 == 0), .by = dealer_id) |>
  filter(round_lakh >= 6)
round_returns
```

```{r}
#| include: false
rr <- round_returns
```

`r if (nrow(rr) == 1) paste0("One dealer, ", dname(rr$dealer_id[1]), ", declared a round lakh in ", rr$round_lakh[1], " of its ", rr$returns[1], " returns. It is the dealer whose buyers report far more.") else paste(Num(nrow(rr)), "dealers declared round lakh in six or more returns.")`

**Duplicate refunds**, @sec-dup-exact. The same claim should not be paid twice.

```{r}
refunds |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = c(dealer_id, refund_type, period)) |>
  nrow()
```

No claim was repeated. A test that finds nothing is also a result, and belongs in the working papers.

**Other chapters.** @sec-recon-itc matched a dealer's credit with its suppliers' returns invoice by invoice, which is the next step for every dealer flagged in @sec-tax-buyers. @sec-dup_net traced many registrations to one person through shared identifiers, at a larger scale than our mobile test. @sec-linkage links lists with no common key, for example the buyers in property documents with the partners of dealers flagged for hiding turnover. A whole State's returns run to crores of rows, and @sec-duckdb shows how to test them. @sec-ts-audit forecasts monthly receipts from past years, to see whether this year's collection is believable.

```{r}
f_round <- round_returns$dealer_id
```

## A risk view of each dealer {#sec-tax-risk}

A dealer caught by one test may have a good reason. One caught by several is a better use of the auditor's time. As in @sec-tenderflags-cri, the simplest way to combine flags is to count them.

```{r}
dealer_flags <- list(
  stopped_filing        = f_stopped,
  moving_after_stopping = f_moving_after,
  nil_while_moving      = f_nil_moving,
  late_six_months       = f_late,
  cancelled_but_moving  = f_cancel_trading,
  movement_above_sales  = f_move_gap,
  buyers_above_sales    = f_buyer_gap,
  tax_fell_trade_grew   = f_drop,
  old_rate_charged      = f_low_rate,
  just_under_limit      = f_near_limit,
  over_limit            = f_over_limit,
  scheme_not_eligible   = f_ineligible,
  refund_when_new       = f_new_refund,
  refund_shared_account = f_shared_acct,
  refund_within_week    = f_fast,
  refund_above_tax_paid = f_above_paid,
  shared_mobile         = f_shared_mobile,
  shared_address        = f_shared_address,
  trading_ring          = f_ring,
  round_lakh_returns    = f_round,
  old_demand            = f_old_demand
)

dealer_risk <- tibble(test = names(dealer_flags), dealer_id = dealer_flags) |>
  unnest(dealer_id) |>
  distinct() |>
  summarise(flags = n(), tests = paste(test, collapse = ", "), .by = dealer_id) |>
  left_join(dealers |> select(dealer_id, dealer_name, trade), by = "dealer_id") |>
  arrange(desc(flags)) |>
  select(dealer_id, dealer_name, flags, tests)

dealer_risk |>
  print(n = 12)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_flagged <- nrow(dealer_risk)
top4 <- dealer_risk |> filter(flags >= 4)
three <- dealer_risk |> filter(flags == 3)
stopper <- mv_after$dealer_id[1]
stopifnot(setequal(top4$dealer_id, c(ring_ids, f_shared_acct, f_nil_moving, stopper)))
stopifnot(setequal(three$dealer_id, c(f_cancel_trading, hide_id, drop_id)), drop_id %in% f_old_demand)
single <- dealer_risk |> filter(flags == 1) |> count(tests, sort = TRUE)
one_flag <- sum(dealer_risk$flags == 1)
```

`tibble()` with a list column, followed by `unnest()`, turns the named list into a long table. `r n_flagged` of `r big(nrow(dealers))` dealers raise at least one flag, and `r one_flag` of them only one. Most single flags are an old demand, a turnover near the limit or a run of late returns. The top of the list is different. The `r num(nrow(top4))` dealers with four or more flags are the four shell dealers, the three new exporters, the nil filer, and the `r str_to_lower(dealers$trade[dealers$dealer_id == stopper])` dealer who stopped filing but kept moving goods. Next, with three flags each, come the two cancelled dealers still trading, the dealer hiding turnover, and the cement dealer whose tax fell, which also has an old demand open. Some serious cases, such as the refund larger than all tax paid or the old rate on tiles, raise only one or two flags. So the count orders the work. It does not decide what to ignore.

A count treats every test as equal. A department with the results of past assessments can do better. @sec-logistic and @sec-trees learn from past cases which flags really go with tax evaded, and so give each a weight. @sec-forest does the same with many more features.

::: callout-note
## A flag is a lead

None of these tests proves evasion. Each says where to look. The work that follows is ordinary audit work, with assessment files, the dealer's books, bank statements and visits. The analysis tests every dealer and every month, and so points that work at the right places.
:::

## Audit use case, a dealer hiding turnover {#sec-tax-case-hiding}

Let us follow `r dname(hide_id)`, the electronics wholesaler whose buyers report far more than it declares. We set its three records side by side, month by month.

```{r}
hide_view <- returns |>
  filter(dealer_id == hide_id) |>
  select(month, declared = turnover, output_tax) |>
  left_join(movement |> filter(dealer_id == hide_id) |> select(month, moved = value_moved), by = "month") |>
  left_join(buyer_reports |> filter(supplier_id == hide_id) |>
              summarise(buyers_report = sum(value), .by = month), by = "month") |>
  mutate(across(c(declared, moved, buyers_report), \(x) round(x / 1e5, 1)))
hide_view |>
  print(n = 12)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
hd <- returns |> filter(dealer_id == hide_id)
hm <- movement |> filter(dealer_id == hide_id)
hb <- buyer_reports |> filter(supplier_id == hide_id)
gap <- sum(hm$value_moved) - sum(hd$turnover)
n_hide_buyers <- n_distinct(hb$buyer_id)
hide_late <- sum(late$days_late[late$dealer_id == hide_id] > 0)
```

The story fits together. In every month the declared turnover is a round lakh, between ₹`r lakh(min(hd$turnover))` lakh and ₹`r lakh(max(hd$turnover))` lakh. In the same months the dealer moved goods worth ₹`r lakh(min(hm$value_moved))` lakh to ₹`r lakh(max(hm$value_moved))` lakh. Its `r num(n_hide_buyers)` registered buyers alone report purchases of ₹`r lakh(sum(hb$value))` lakh for the year, against ₹`r lakh(sum(hd$turnover))` lakh declared. Three independent records point the same way. The goods moved exceed the turnover declared by ₹`r lakh(gap)` lakh. If all of that was sold at 18%, the output tax on it would be about ₹`r lakh(0.18 * gap)` lakh, before any further credit the dealer can prove. That figure is an estimate to guide the work. The assessment will fix the real one.

Why did nobody notice? The dealer filed every return`r if (hide_late == 0) " on time" else ""`, and paid what it declared. Every test of filing passes. Only the third-party records show the gap.

### What the auditor does next

1. Ask for the **assessment records** of the dealer. Was the return ever scrutinised, and were the buyers' reports and movement records before the officer?
2. Ask the officer to call for the **dealer's books**, stock register and sales invoices, and to match them with the movement records consignment by consignment.
3. Pick a few large buyers and match their purchase invoices with the dealer's sales, as in @sec-recon-itc.
4. Ask for the dealer's **bank statements**. Receipts far above the declared sales confirm the case.
5. If the gap is confirmed, the department raises a demand for the tax, interest and penalty. Report the case, and the wider point that returns are accepted without a look at third-party data.

## Audit use case, refunds to a ring of new dealers {#sec-tax-case-refunds}

Let us follow the three "exporters" who share a refund account. Account numbers are masked, as in @sec-privacy-mask.

```{r}
trio_ids <- f_shared_acct
mask <- function(x) paste0("XXXXXXXX", str_sub(x, -4))

dealers |>
  filter(dealer_id %in% trio_ids) |>
  mutate(account = mask(bank_account)) |>
  select(dealer_name, district, reg_date, mobile, account)
```

Where did their credit come from? The buyers' reports show who sold to them.

```{r}
buyer_reports |>
  filter(buyer_id %in% trio_ids) |>
  summarise(months = n_distinct(month), bought_lakh = round(sum(value) / 1e5, 1),
            .by = c(supplier_id, buyer_id)) |>
  mutate(supplier = dname(supplier_id), buyer = dname(buyer_id)) |>
  select(supplier, buyer, months, bought_lakh)

returns |>
  filter(dealer_id %in% trio_ids) |>
  summarise(exports = sum(export_value), itc_claimed = sum(itc_claimed), .by = dealer_id) |>
  left_join(movement |> summarise(moved = sum(value_moved), .by = dealer_id), by = "dealer_id") |>
  left_join(refunds |> summarise(refunded = sum(amount_sanctioned, na.rm = TRUE), .by = dealer_id),
            by = "dealer_id") |>
  mutate(dealer = dname(dealer_id)) |>
  select(dealer, exports, itc_claimed, moved, refunded)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
trio_sup <- buyer_reports |> filter(buyer_id %in% trio_ids) |> distinct(supplier_id)
trio_ref <- refunds |> filter(dealer_id %in% trio_ids)
trio_moved <- sum(movement$value_moved[movement$dealer_id %in% trio_ids])
trio_exports <- sum(returns$export_value[returns$dealer_id %in% trio_ids])
trio_days <- range(as.numeric(trio_ref$sanction_date - trio_ref$claim_date), na.rm = TRUE)
stopifnot(all(trio_sup$supplier_id %in% ring_ids))
```

The pieces join up. The three registered within `r as.numeric(diff(range(dealers$reg_date[dealers$dealer_id %in% trio_ids])))` days of each other in November. All their purchases came from `r if (nrow(trio_sup) == 1) dname(trio_sup$supplier_id[1]) else "the ring"`, one of the four shell dealers trading in a circle. They declared exports of ₹`r crore(trio_exports)` crore, yet `r if (trio_moved == 0) "not one consignment of theirs appears in the movement records" else "their movement records are small"`. Their credit, built on invoices from a ring that never moved goods, came back as `r num(nrow(trio_ref))` refunds of ₹`r lakh(sum(trio_ref$amount_sanctioned, na.rm = TRUE))` lakh, sanctioned in `r trio_days[1]` to `r trio_days[2]` days, into one bank account. Credit went round the ring, and came out as cash.

Each test alone found a piece. The refund tests found new dealers, a shared account and a quick sanction. The shell tests found shared identifiers and a circle. Only together do they show the scheme.

### What the auditor does next

1. Ask for the **refund files**. Who sanctioned each refund, what was checked, and why so fast? Were export documents such as shipping bills on file and verified?
2. Ask for the **registering officer's file** of all seven dealers. Who verified the premises and the identity of the proprietors, and when?
3. Ask the bank, through the department, for the **account holder** and the statement of the refund account. Where did the money go next?
4. Arrange a **physical verification** of the business premises of all seven at the addresses given, with the local officer.
5. If confirmed, the department should recover the refunds, block the credit passed by the ring, and cancel the registrations. Report the case, and the control weakness of refunds sanctioned without a look at the claimant's age, suppliers and identifiers.

## A suggested workflow

1. **Get the full data**, including movement records, buyers' reports, the rate master, refund and demand registers, and the property documents. Record who extracted it and when.
2. **Check completeness.** A unique key, every return linked to a dealer, and tax paid agreeing with the treasury.
3. **Test filing.** Returns expected against received, dealers who stopped, nil returns, late returns, and cancelled dealers still trading.
4. **Compare declarations with third-party data.** Movement records, buyers' reports and the trend of the trade.
5. **Check rates, limits and concessions.** The rate in force, bunching below a limit, and eligibility for a scheme.
6. **Test refunds.** New claimants, shared accounts, fast sanctions, and refunds above the tax or credit.
7. **Look for shell dealers.** Shared identifiers, short lives and circles of trade.
8. **Test stamp duty and demands.** Guideline values, duplicates, property type, and the age of open demands.
9. **Add the tests of earlier chapters,** combine the flags for each dealer, and follow up the top cases on paper and in person.

::: callout-important
## Remember

- Revenue audit looks for money not collected. The loss shows only when a return is read against another record.
- Count the returns expected against those received. A dealer who stops filing, or files nil, while goods move is still trading.
- Movement records and buyers' reports put a floor under a dealer's sales. Compare them over a year, to allow for timing.
- Use a rolling join to find the rate in force on each date.
- Concessions with limits invite bunching just below them. A histogram shows it.
- Refunds turn credit into cash. Look at the claimant's age, account, suppliers and the speed of sanction.
- Many flags have innocent causes. Several flags on one dealer deserve the auditor's time.
:::

## Where next

Reconciliation of credit with suppliers' returns is in @sec-recon-itc, and the rate in force in @sec-joins-audit. Circular trading and shared identifiers are in @sec-netaudit. Time series and change points are in @sec-ts and @sec-ano-changepoint. Models that learn from past assessments are in @sec-logistic, @sec-trees and @sec-forest. Duplicates are in @sec-dup, string similarity in @sec-strsim, and Benford's law and Nigrini's tests in @sec-benford and @sec-nigrini. Large data is in @sec-duckdb, and personal data in @sec-privacy. @sec-ssyaudit, next, audits a whole scheme.

## Try it yourself {#sec-tax-exercises}

These exercises use the objects of this chapter. Try each before opening the solution.

1.  **Why compare with the trade?** Repeat the test of @sec-tax-trend without the condition that the trade grew, and with a looser cut of 0.7 instead of 0.5. Which trades do the extra dealers come from, and why?

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_drops <- halves |>
      summarise(tax = sum(output_tax), months = n(), .by = c(dealer_id, trade, half)) |>
      pivot_wider(names_from = half, values_from = c(tax, months)) |>
      filter(months_first == 6, months_second == 6, tax_first > 0) |>
      mutate(change = tax_second / tax_first) |>
      filter(change < 0.7)
    ex_drops |>
      count(trade, sort = TRUE)
    ```
    `r Num(nrow(ex_drops))` dealers fall below 0.7. `r sum(ex_drops$trade == "Fertiliser")` of them sell fertiliser, whose sales fall in the second half every year. They are seasonal, not suspicious. Comparing each dealer with its own trade removes them`r if (setequal(ex_drops$dealer_id[ex_drops$trade != "Fertiliser"], drops$dealer_id)) ", and leaves the two real cases" else ""`.
    :::

2.  **Late fee due.** Suppose, as an example norm, that a late return attracts a fee of ₹50 a day, up to ₹5,000 a return. Work out the fee due on all late returns, and the dealer with the most.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_fee <- late |>
      filter(days_late > 0) |>
      mutate(fee = pmin(50 * days_late, 5000))
    sum(ex_fee$fee)
    ex_fee |>
      summarise(fee = sum(fee), late_returns = n(), .by = dealer_id) |>
      slice_max(fee, n = 1)
    ```
    The fee due comes to ₹`r lakh(sum(ex_fee$fee))` lakh. The next step is to match it with the fees actually paid, which the returns data would have to include.
    :::

3.  **The old rate in the returns.** The returns of building material dealers show taxable value at 12% and 18%. Tiles moved to 18% from October, so the share at 12% should fall. Find the dealers whose share at 12% stayed above 30% from October.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_share <- returns |>
      inner_join(dealers |> filter(trade == "Building material", scheme == "Regular") |> select(dealer_id),
                 by = "dealer_id") |>
      filter(month >= as.Date("2024-10-01")) |>
      summarise(share_12 = sum(taxable_12) / sum(taxable_5 + taxable_12 + taxable_18), .by = dealer_id) |>
      filter(share_12 > 0.3)
    ex_share
    ```
    `r if (nrow(ex_share) == 1 && ex_share$dealer_id[1] %in% f_low_rate) "Only the dealer found from the invoices appears. Its returns confirm that all its tile sales stayed at 12%, not only the invoices we saw." else paste(Num(nrow(ex_share)), "dealers appear.")`
    :::

4.  **Stamp duty by month.** For the documents below the guideline value that were not referred, show the number of documents and the duty short-levied by month of registration.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_month <- below |>
      filter(referred == "No") |>
      mutate(month = floor_date(reg_date, "month")) |>
      summarise(documents = n(), short_levy = sum(short_levy), .by = month) |>
      arrange(month)
    ex_month
    ```
    All the documents fall between `r fmonth(min(ex_month$month))` and `r fmonth(max(ex_month$month))`. A burst like this points to one period in the office, and the auditor should ask who registered them.
    :::

5.  **Old demands by district.** Take the open demands that are not stayed and are already barred or reach the limit in 2025-26. Total their balance by the district of the dealer.

    ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
    ## Solution
    ```{r}
    ex_district <- bind_rows(barred, nearing) |>
      left_join(dealers |> select(dealer_id, district), by = "dealer_id") |>
      summarise(demands = n(), balance_lakh = round(sum(balance) / 1e5, 1), .by = district) |>
      arrange(desc(balance_lakh))
    ex_district
    ```
    `r ex_district$district[1]` holds the largest balance, ₹`r ex_district$balance_lakh[1]` lakh. A table like this tells the department where to send its recovery staff first.
    :::

## Summary of functions used

| Function | Package | What it does |
|-----------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| `anyDuplicated()` | base R | Checks that the dealer key is unique |
| `anti_join()`, `semi_join()` | dplyr | Finds returns expected but not received, and stray returns |
| `cross_join()` | dplyr | Pairs every dealer with every month, to list the returns expected |
| `inner_join()`, `left_join()` | dplyr | Brings returns, movement, buyers' reports, refunds and demands together |
| `join_by()` with `closest()` | dplyr | Finds the rate in force on the date of each invoice |
| `filter(n() > 1, .by = )` | dplyr | Finds shared mobiles, shared refund accounts and properties registered twice |
| `lag()` | dplyr | Compares each sale of a property with the one before |
| `pivot_wider()`, `unnest()` | tidyr | Puts two halves of the year side by side, and turns a list of flags into a table |
| `str_replace_all()`, `str_remove()`, `str_extract()` | stringr | Standardises addresses and takes out the house number |
| `str_detect()` with `regex()` | stringr | Finds shops described in documents registered as houses |
| `stringdist()` | stringdist | Distance between two addresses |
| `graph_from_data_frame()`, `components()` | igraph | Builds the network of trade and finds dealers trading in a circle |
| `floor_date()`, `%m+%`, `months()`, `years()` | lubridate | Return months, due dates and the time limit of a demand |
| `interval()`, `time_length()` | lubridate | Months from registration to a refund claim, and the age of a demand |
| `geom_histogram()`, `geom_line()` | ggplot2 | Shows bunching below a limit, and a dealer's tax against its trade |
| `cut()` | base R | Puts turnovers and demands into bands |
